course.title: React + TypeScript Full-Stack Mastery
course.description: A comprehensive 40-part course taking you from absolute beginner to confident full-stack developer using React 18+, TypeScript 5+, and modern tooling. Covers component architecture, hooks, state management with Zustand/Redux, React Router, API integration with TanStack Query, testing with Vitest, and a complete capstone SaaS project.

blocks.value: Understanding React

React is a **declarative**, **component-based** JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Developed by Meta (formerly Facebook) and released in 2013, React introduced the concept of the **Virtual DOM** — a lightweight in-memory representation of the actual DOM that enables efficient UI updates without directly manipulating the browser's DOM tree.

blocks.alt: React logo and component tree visualization
blocks.caption: React's component-based architecture allows you to build complex UIs from small, isolated pieces.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A clean, modern infographic showing the React logo (atom-like symbol) at the top center, with branching component trees below. Each node is a rounded rectangle representing a component (Header, Sidebar, MainContent, Footer). Arrows show unidirectional data flow. Color palette: React blue (#61DAFB), dark navy background (#282C34), white text. Flat design style with subtle shadows. 16:9 aspect ratio.
Why React + TypeScript?

While React works with plain JavaScript, pairing it with **TypeScript** provides compile-time type safety, better IDE autocomplete, and self-documenting code. TypeScript catches errors before they reach production — a game-changer for large applications. React 18+ has first-class TypeScript support, making the developer experience seamless.

blocks.output: Renders a heading "Hello, [name]!" and optionally displays the age if provided. TypeScript ensures the `name` prop is always a string and `age` is optional.

blocks.value: The Virtual DOM Explained

When state changes, React creates a new Virtual DOM tree, compares it with the previous one using a **diffing algorithm** (reconciliation), and updates only the changed nodes in the real DOM. This minimizes expensive DOM operations and keeps your app fast.

blocks.output: Renders a button showing "Count: 0". Each click increments the number. React efficiently updates only the text node inside the button, not the entire DOM tree.

blocks.question: What is the primary purpose of React's Virtual DOM?
options: To replace the browser's DOM entirely
To minimize direct DOM manipulation for better performance
blocks.explanation: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight copy of the real DOM. React uses it to compare changes and update only the necessary parts of the actual DOM, avoiding expensive full re-renders.

blocks.question: Which of the following are core principles of React? (Select all that apply)
blocks.explanation: React is declarative (you describe what the UI should look like), component-based (UI built from reusable pieces), and uses unidirectional data flow (data flows down via props). Two-way binding is not a React default — it requires explicit handler wiring.

blocks.question: What is the name of the algorithm React uses to compare the new Virtual DOM with the previous one?
blocks.explanation: Reconciliation is React's diffing algorithm that determines the minimal set of changes needed to update the real DOM when state or props change.

blocks.question: In the TypeScript interface `GreetingProps`, what does the `?` symbol indicate for the `age` property?
blocks.explanation: In TypeScript, the `?` symbol after a property name makes it optional. So `age?: number` means the `age` prop can be provided or omitted when using the component.

blocks.question: What does `React.FC<GreetingProps>` signify in the component declaration?
options: It creates a new React context
It defines a functional component with typed props
It registers the component as a forward ref
It enables server-side rendering for the component
blocks.explanation: `React.FC<Props>` is a generic type alias that stands for React Function Component. It types the component's props and automatically includes `children` in the type definition (though modern practice often avoids it).

parts.partTitle: Part 2: Setting Up Your Dev Environment

blocks.value: Creating a React + TypeScript Project

The fastest way to start a modern React + TypeScript project is with **Vite** — a next-generation build tool that provides instant server start and lightning-fast HMR (Hot Module Replacement). Vite replaces the older Create React App (CRA) toolchain and is now the industry standard.

# Create a new React + TypeScript project with Vite
npm create vite@latest my-react-app -- --template react-ts

# Navigate into the project
cd my-react-app

# Install dependencies
npm install

# Start the development server
npm run dev
blocks.output: Vite scaffolds a project with TypeScript configured, creates a `src/` directory with `App.tsx` and `main.tsx`, installs dependencies, and starts a dev server at `http://localhost:5173`.

blocks.alt: VS Code editor with React TypeScript code
blocks.caption: A well-configured IDE with IntelliSense, ESLint, and Prettier dramatically improves your React + TypeScript workflow.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Screenshot-style mockup of VS Code showing a split view. Left pane: file explorer with `src/components/Button.tsx` highlighted. Right pane: code editor with syntax-highlighted TypeScript React code showing a Button component with typed props. Bottom panel shows terminal with Vite dev server running. Theme: Dark mode (VS Code Dark+). Color accents: React blue for JSX tags, orange for strings, cyan for types. Clean, professional developer workspace aesthetic.
Essential Tooling Configuration

For a professional setup, configure **ESLint** with TypeScript support, **Prettier** for code formatting, and **Path Aliases** for clean imports. These tools catch bugs early and enforce consistent code style across your team.

blocks.output: Enables clean imports like `import { Button } from '@components/Button'` instead of relative paths like `../../../components/Button`. The IDE resolves these automatically.
Vite now recognizes `@/` and `@components/` aliases at build time, bundling the correct files while keeping your import statements clean and refactor-friendly.

blocks.value: Project Structure Best Practices
A well-organized project structure scales with your application. Group by **feature** rather than by file type — this keeps related code together and makes navigation intuitive as your app grows.

my-react-app/
├── src/
│   ├── components/          # Reusable UI components
│   │   ├── Button/
│   │   │   ├── Button.tsx
│   │   │   ├── Button.test.tsx
│   │   │   └── Button.module.css
│   ├── features/            # Feature-specific modules
│   │   └── auth/
│   │       ├── LoginForm.tsx
│   │       └── useAuth.ts
│   ├── hooks/               # Custom React hooks
│   ├── types/               # Shared TypeScript types
│   ├── utils/               # Helper functions
│   ├── App.tsx
│   └── main.tsx
├── public/
├── index.html
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
└── vite.config.ts
blocks.output: A scalable project structure where each feature (auth, dashboard, etc.) contains its own components, hooks, and types. This co-location pattern prevents import spaghetti and makes code ownership clear.

blocks.question: Which tool is recommended for scaffolding a modern React + TypeScript project?
blocks.explanation: Vite with the `react-ts` template is the modern standard. It provides faster dev server startup, instant HMR, and a leaner configuration compared to the now-deprecated Create React App.

blocks.question: Which of the following are benefits of using path aliases in a React + TypeScript project? (Select all that apply)
blocks.explanation: Path aliases make imports cleaner (`@components/Button` vs `../../../components/Button`), simplify refactoring (move files without changing imports), and improve IDE support. They do not directly affect build performance.

blocks.question: In the Vite config, which Node.js module is used to resolve absolute paths for aliases?
blocks.explanation: The Node.js `path` module (specifically `path.resolve`) is used to create absolute paths from relative ones, ensuring aliases point to the correct directories regardless of where the config file is located.

blocks.question: What is the recommended project organization strategy for scaling React applications?
options: Group all components in one folder, all hooks in another, all types in another
Group by file type (.tsx, .ts, .css) in separate top-level folders
Group by feature, co-locating related components, hooks, and types
Keep everything in a single src folder with no subdirectories
blocks.explanation: Feature-based organization co-locates related code (components, hooks, types) within feature folders (e.g., `features/auth/`). This scales better than grouping by file type because it keeps related code together and makes navigation intuitive.

blocks.question: What does HMR stand for in the context of Vite's development server?
blocks.explanation: Hot Module Replacement (HMR) allows modules to be updated in the browser at runtime without a full page refresh. Vite provides instant HMR, preserving component state during development.

blocks.value: Understanding JSX and TSX

**JSX** (JavaScript XML) is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like code inside JavaScript. **TSX** is the TypeScript version of JSX, giving you the same expressive syntax with full type safety. Under the hood, JSX/TSX compiles to `React.createElement()` calls.

blocks.output: Both snippets produce the same React element object. TSX is syntactic sugar that makes component code readable and declarative while TypeScript enforces type correctness.

blocks.caption: TSX syntax is transformed by the compiler into nested React.createElement() calls that build the Virtual DOM tree.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A split-screen diagram. Left side: clean TSX code showing a nested component tree (`<Card><Header /><Body /></Card>`). A large curved arrow points to the right side showing the compiled output: nested `React.createElement()` calls forming a tree structure. Each node is color-coded by type (blue for HTML elements, green for components, orange for props). Clean vector illustration style on a light gray background. Labels in monospace font.
JSX Rules and Gotchas

JSX has a few important rules: you must return a **single root element** (or use fragments), use `className` instead of `class`, and wrap JavaScript expressions in curly braces `{}`. All tags must be closed, including self-closing tags like ``.

blocks.output: Renders a card div with dynamic className (includes 'active' when isActive is true), interpolated userName, conditional status text, and an image with a dynamically generated alt attribute. The Fragment (`<>...</>`) avoids adding an unnecessary wrapper element to the DOM.

blocks.value: TypeScript in TSX: Typing JSX Elements

TypeScript provides specific types for JSX. `JSX.Element` represents a single React element, `React.ReactNode` accepts elements, strings, numbers, and arrays — making it the most flexible type for children. Use `React.ReactElement` when you need to be specific about the component type.

blocks.output: Renders a div with class 'wrapper' containing an h1, a p tag, and the number 42 as text. TypeScript ensures only valid ReactNode values are passed as children.

blocks.question: What does TSX compile to under the hood?
blocks.explanation: TSX is syntactic sugar that transpiles to `React.createElement()` calls. These calls return plain JavaScript objects (React elements) that describe what should appear on screen.

blocks.question: Which of the following are valid JSX/TSX rules? (Select all that apply)
options: Use `className` instead of `class` for CSS classes
Wrap JavaScript expressions in curly braces `{}`
Return multiple root elements without a wrapper
Close all tags, including self-closing ones
blocks.explanation: In JSX, you must use `className` (class is a reserved JS keyword), wrap expressions in `{}`, and close all tags. You cannot return multiple root elements without a wrapper (Fragment or container element).

blocks.question: What TypeScript type accepts the widest range of valid React children (elements, strings, numbers, arrays)?
blocks.explanation: `React.ReactNode` is the most inclusive type for children — it accepts JSX elements, strings, numbers, fragments, portals, and arrays of these. `JSX.Element` is more restrictive, only accepting single elements.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of the empty tag syntax `<>...</>` in React?
options: It creates a new HTML5 custom element
It is a React Fragment that groups children without adding extra DOM nodes
It comments out the enclosed JSX
It forces a re-render of the component
blocks.explanation: `<>...</>` is shorthand for `<React.Fragment>...</React.Fragment>`. It allows returning multiple elements from a component without wrapping them in an extra div or other DOM element.

blocks.question: In TSX, why must you use `className` instead of `class` for CSS classes?
options: It is a React convention with no technical reason
`class` is a reserved keyword in JavaScript/TypeScript
TypeScript does not support the `class` attribute
It prevents conflicts with CSS modules
blocks.explanation: `class` is a reserved keyword in JavaScript (used for ES6 classes). JSX/TSX transpiles to JavaScript, so using `class` would cause syntax errors. `className` is the JSX equivalent.

blocks.value: Functional Components in TypeScript

In modern React, **functional components** are the standard. Combined with TypeScript, they provide clear contracts for props, return types, and state. A functional component is simply a function that accepts props and returns JSX.

blocks.output: Renders a button with dynamic CSS class based on the variant prop (e.g., 'btn btn--primary'). TypeScript enforces that label is a string, variant is one of three literal values, and onClick is an optional function. Default values ensure the component works even with partial props.

blocks.alt: Component composition diagram showing parent and child components
blocks.caption: Components compose together like LEGO blocks — each piece is self-contained and reusable.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: An isometric 3D illustration of component composition. A large 'App' block at the top connects downward to medium-sized blocks labeled 'Header', 'Sidebar', 'MainContent'. Each medium block further connects to smaller blocks (e.g., 'MainContent' → 'Card', 'Card' → 'Button', 'Avatar'). Blocks are colored in a cohesive palette (React blue, teal, coral, purple). Connection lines are dotted and animated-looking. Clean, modern flat-3D style on a soft gradient background.
Component Composition with Children

The real power of React lies in **composition** — building complex UIs by nesting simpler components. The `children` prop is the primary mechanism for composition, allowing you to wrap components around content.

blocks.output: Renders an article with a header containing the title, a body with the provided children paragraphs, and a footer with an Edit button. The Card component is reusable with any content passed as children or footer.

blocks.value: Destructuring Props for Clean Code

Destructuring props in the function parameter makes your components more readable. You can also provide default values inline, reducing boilerplate and making the component's interface self-documenting.

blocks.output: Renders a span with classes 'badge badge--green badge--md' containing the text 'New'. Default values ensure the component renders correctly even when optional props are omitted.

blocks.question: What is the primary mechanism for component composition in React?
options: Inheritance from a base Component class
blocks.explanation: The `children` prop is React's primary composition mechanism. It allows components to wrap and render nested content, enabling flexible and reusable component design without inheritance.

blocks.question: Which of the following are benefits of typing props with TypeScript interfaces? (Select all that apply)
options: Compile-time error detection for missing or wrong props
blocks.explanation: TypeScript interfaces provide compile-time checking, IDE autocomplete, and self-documenting code. However, TypeScript types are erased at runtime — they do not provide automatic runtime validation (use PropTypes or Zod for that).

blocks.question: In the Button component, what TypeScript syntax is used to restrict the `variant` prop to only three specific string values?
blocks.explanation: The syntax `'primary' | 'secondary' | 'danger'` is a TypeScript union type. It restricts the prop to exactly those three literal string values, providing both type safety and autocomplete.

blocks.question: Why is destructuring props in the function parameter considered a best practice?
options: It makes the component code cleaner and props immediately visible
blocks.explanation: Destructuring in the parameter list makes the component's props immediately visible at the top of the function, improves readability, and allows setting default values inline. It has no impact on runtime performance or SSR.

blocks.question: What happens if you pass a prop value that is not in the union type to a typed component?
options: The component falls back to a default value
blocks.explanation: TypeScript will show a compile-time error (red squiggly underline in the IDE) if you pass an invalid prop value like `variant='ghost'` when only 'primary', 'secondary', and 'danger' are allowed. This catches bugs before runtime.

blocks.value: Advanced Prop Typing Patterns

As your components grow in complexity, you'll need advanced TypeScript patterns: **optional props**, **union types**, **intersection types**, and **generic components**. These patterns let you build flexible, reusable components with strict type safety.

blocks.output: Renders an alert with dynamic styling based on type. TypeScript enforces that 'error' alerts MUST include an errorCode and title, while 'info' alerts have an optional title, and 'success' alerts have an optional autoDismiss. Invalid prop combinations are caught at compile time.

blocks.alt: TypeScript type system visualization showing union and intersection types
blocks.caption: Discriminated unions let you create components with different prop requirements based on a type discriminator.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A Venn diagram-style visualization showing TypeScript type operations. Three overlapping circles labeled 'BaseAlertProps', 'InfoProps', 'ErrorProps', 'SuccessProps'. The intersection areas are highlighted in different colors showing how intersection types (`&`) combine properties. Arrows point from a 'type' discriminator to the correct prop shape. Clean vector illustration with TypeScript blue (#3178C6) accents. Monospace font for code snippets embedded in the diagram.
Event Handling with Typed Events

React wraps native DOM events in **SyntheticEvent** objects. TypeScript provides specific event types for different handlers — `React.MouseEvent`, `React.ChangeEvent`, `React.FormEvent`, and more. Using the correct type gives you full autocomplete for event properties.

blocks.output: Renders a form with two controlled inputs. Typing in either field updates the corresponding state property. On submit, the form prevents default browser behavior and logs the form data. TypeScript ensures `e.target` has the correct properties for each event type.

blocks.value: Spreading Props and Rest Parameters

Use the **rest parameter** pattern (`...rest`) to forward unknown props to underlying elements. This is especially useful for wrapper components that need to pass HTML attributes through while adding their own behavior.

blocks.output: Renders a button with a right-positioned arrow icon and the text 'Submit'. All native button attributes (onClick, disabled, type) are forwarded via `...rest`. TypeScript ensures only valid button attributes and IconButton-specific props are accepted.

blocks.question: What TypeScript pattern is used to create components where different variants require different props?
blocks.explanation: Discriminated unions use a common 'type' or 'variant' property to determine which specific props are required. TypeScript narrows the type based on the discriminator value, ensuring correct props for each variant.

blocks.question: Which of the following are valid React event types in TypeScript? (Select all that apply)
blocks.explanation: `React.MouseEvent`, `React.ChangeEvent`, and `React.FormEvent` are all valid React SyntheticEvent types. `React.DOMEvent` is not a valid type — the generic form is `React.SyntheticEvent`.

blocks.question: What TypeScript utility type allows a component to accept all native HTML button attributes plus custom props?
blocks.explanation: Using `interface MyProps extends ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement>` (or `extends React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>`) allows your component to accept all native button attributes while adding custom ones.

blocks.question: What does the `...rest` pattern achieve in the IconButton component?
options: It creates a new state variable
It forwards all remaining props to the underlying button element
blocks.explanation: The rest parameter (`...rest`) collects all props not explicitly destructured (like icon, iconPosition, children) and spreads them onto the native `<button>` element. This passes through standard HTML attributes like `disabled`, `type`, and `aria-label`.

blocks.question: In the LoginForm, what is the purpose of `e.preventDefault()` in the handleSubmit function?
options: It prevents TypeScript from checking the event type
It stops the form from submitting and reloading the page
It prevents the component from re-rendering
blocks.explanation: `e.preventDefault()` prevents the browser's default form submission behavior (which would cause a full page reload). This allows React to handle the submission with JavaScript, typically sending data to an API without refreshing the page.

blocks.value: The useState Hook

`useState` is the fundamental hook for adding state to functional components. It returns a tuple: the current state value and a setter function. TypeScript can infer the state type from the initial value, but you should provide an explicit generic for complex types or when the initial value is `null` or `undefined`.

blocks.output: Renders a counter and conditional user profile. `count` is inferred as number. `user` is typed as `User | null` — TypeScript requires null checks before accessing `user.name`. `setCount(prev => prev + 1)` uses the functional update pattern to avoid stale state in async operations.

blocks.caption: useState creates a reactive value that triggers re-renders when updated via the setter function.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A state machine diagram showing a component box labeled 'UserProfile'. Inside, a circle labeled 'useState' contains the current value (e.g., 'count: 0'). An arrow labeled 'setCount(1)' points to a new circle with 'count: 1', which triggers a re-render arrow back to the component. Colors: React blue for state, orange for setter calls, green for re-render flow. Clean vector illustration with animated-style arrows. Light background.
The useEffect Hook

`useEffect` handles side effects in functional components — data fetching, subscriptions, DOM manipulation, and timers. It runs after every render by default, but you control when it fires via the **dependency array**. An empty array `[]` means "run once on mount."

blocks.output: Fetches posts on component mount, showing a loading state, then renders a list of posts. The cleanup function with a `cancelled` flag prevents state updates if the component unmounts before the fetch completes — preventing memory leaks and React warnings.

blocks.value: Effect Dependencies and Stale Closures

The dependency array is the most common source of bugs in React. Missing dependencies cause **stale closures** — effects that use old values. The ESLint `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` rule catches most issues, but understanding the mechanics is essential.

blocks.output: Renders a timer that increments every second when running. The cleanup function clears the interval when `isRunning` changes to false or the component unmounts. Using the functional update `setCount(c => c + 1)` avoids adding `count` to the dependency array.

blocks.question: What does the empty dependency array `[]` in useEffect mean?
options: The effect runs after every render
The effect runs only once when the component mounts
The effect runs before every render
blocks.explanation: An empty dependency array `[]` tells React to run the effect only once — after the initial render (mount). It's equivalent to `componentDidMount` in class components.

blocks.question: Which of the following are valid strategies to avoid stale closures in useEffect? (Select all that apply)
options: Include all used values in the dependency array
Use functional updates for state setters
Use refs for values that shouldn't trigger re-renders
Always use an empty dependency array
blocks.explanation: Including all dependencies ensures effects use current values. Functional updates (`setCount(c => c + 1)`) avoid needing the state in dependencies. Refs store mutable values without causing re-renders. Empty arrays should only be used when truly appropriate.

blocks.question: What is the name of the pattern where you pass a function to the state setter instead of a direct value?
blocks.explanation: A functional update passes a function to the setter (e.g., `setCount(prev => prev + 1)`). React calls this function with the previous state value, ensuring you always work with the latest state — critical for async operations and effects.

blocks.question: Why is the `cancelled` flag used in the fetch effect's cleanup function?
options: To prevent state updates on an unmounted component
blocks.explanation: The `cancelled` flag is a boolean ref that the cleanup function sets to true on unmount. The effect checks this flag before calling setState, preventing updates to an unmounted component which would cause a React warning.

blocks.question: What TypeScript generic should you use when useState's initial value is `null` but the state will later hold an object?
blocks.explanation: You should explicitly provide the union type: `useState<TheObjectType | null>(null)`. This tells TypeScript that the state is either null or the specific object type, enabling proper type narrowing and autocomplete when you check for null.

blocks.value: Understanding useRef

`useRef` creates a **mutable reference** that persists across re-renders without causing re-renders when changed. It has two primary uses: accessing DOM elements directly and storing mutable values (timers, previous state, interval IDs) that don't need to trigger UI updates.

blocks.output: Renders an input that auto-focuses on mount, a button that selects all text, and a render counter. `inputRef` holds a reference to the DOM input element. `renderCount` tracks renders without causing infinite re-render loops because ref changes don't trigger re-renders.

blocks.alt: useRef hook visualization showing DOM reference and mutable value
blocks.caption: useRef creates a persistent box that survives re-renders — perfect for DOM access and mutable state that shouldn't trigger UI updates.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A diagram showing a React component as a box. Inside, two labeled containers: 'DOM Ref' pointing to an HTML input element (shown as a small browser input mockup), and 'Mutable Value' containing a counter '5'. Arrows show re-render cycles passing by the containers without touching them — they remain stable across renders. One arrow shows a direct DOM manipulation (focus) from the ref to the input. Clean vector style with React blue and gray tones. Isometric perspective.
Storing Previous Values with useRef
A common pattern uses `useRef` to store the previous value of a prop or state. Since refs update synchronously (unlike state), they capture values before the current render completes.

blocks.output: Renders current count, previous count, and the difference. After each render, the effect updates `prevCountRef` with the current count. On the next render, `prevCount` shows the value from before the latest state update.

blocks.value: Forwarding Refs to Child Components

By default, refs don't pass through components. `forwardRef` lets child components receive a ref and forward it to a DOM element. Combined with `useImperativeHandle`, you can expose custom methods on the ref.

blocks.output: Renders a labeled input and three buttons. The parent accesses the child's input via `fancyRef` to focus it, clear its value, or read its current value. `useImperativeHandle` exposes only the specified methods, keeping the internal DOM ref encapsulated.

blocks.question: What is the key difference between useState and useRef?
options: useRef can only store DOM elements
useRef persists across renders without causing re-renders
useState is synchronous while useRef is async
useRef is only available in class components
blocks.explanation: useRef returns a mutable object whose `.current` property persists across renders. Changing it does NOT trigger a re-render, unlike useState. This makes refs ideal for DOM access and values that don't need UI updates.

blocks.question: Which of the following are valid use cases for useRef? (Select all that apply)
blocks.explanation: useRef is perfect for DOM access, storing mutable values like timers, and tracking previous values. It should NOT be used to trigger re-renders — that's what useState is for.

blocks.question: What hook allows a child component to expose custom methods to its parent via a ref?
blocks.explanation: `useImperativeHandle` customizes the instance value that is exposed when parent components use `ref`. It's used with `forwardRef` to expose specific methods rather than the entire DOM node.

blocks.question: Why must `FancyInput.displayName` be set when using forwardRef?
options: It provides a readable name in React DevTools and error messages
It is required for the ref to work
blocks.explanation: When using forwardRef, the component name is often lost in minification or shown as 'ForwardRef' in DevTools. Setting `displayName` provides a human-readable name for debugging and stack traces.

blocks.question: What happens if you read `renderCount.current` during render (not in an effect)?
options: It reads the value from the previous render
It always returns the initial value
blocks.explanation: Refs are updated synchronously, but the component function reads the ref value during render. Since effects run after render, reading during render gets the value from the previous render cycle. This is why the 'previous value' pattern works.

blocks.value: Building Reusable Custom Hooks

**Custom hooks** extract component logic into reusable functions. They follow the same rules as built-in hooks (must start with `use`, can only call other hooks at the top level). Custom hooks are the primary mechanism for sharing stateful logic between components without render props or HOCs.

blocks.output: The `useFetch` hook encapsulates all data fetching logic: loading states, error handling, and refetch capability. Multiple components can use `useFetch` with different URLs and types, each maintaining independent state. The `useCallback` ensures the fetch function is stable across renders.

blocks.caption: Custom hooks extract logic from components, making it reusable across your application while keeping components focused on presentation.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A diagram showing three component boxes (UserList, ProductList, OrderList) all connecting to a central cylinder labeled 'useFetch<T>'. Each component passes a different URL and receives typed data. The hook cylinder contains smaller gears labeled 'useState', 'useEffect', 'useCallback'. Arrows show data flowing back to components with loading, error, and data states. Clean vector illustration with a plumbing/pipes metaphor. React blue and teal colors.
useLocalStorage Hook

A `useLocalStorage` hook synchronizes state with the browser's localStorage, providing persistence across page reloads. It handles JSON serialization, SSR safety, and storage events for cross-tab synchronization.

blocks.output: The theme preference persists across page reloads and syncs across browser tabs. The hook handles SSR (checks `typeof window`), JSON parsing/stringification, and the `storage` event for cross-tab communication. The setter accepts both direct values and updater functions.

blocks.value: useDebounce Hook

Debouncing delays function execution until after a period of inactivity. A `useDebounce` hook is essential for search inputs, resize handlers, and any scenario where rapid events shouldn't trigger expensive operations.

blocks.output: The search input updates immediately, but the API call only fires 500ms after the user stops typing. The cleanup function clears the previous timer on each keystroke, ensuring only the final debounced value triggers the fetch.

blocks.question: What is the naming convention for custom hooks in React?
blocks.explanation: Custom hooks must start with 'use' (e.g., useFetch, useLocalStorage). This convention allows React's ESLint rules to enforce the Rules of Hooks — ensuring hooks are only called at the top level of functions.

blocks.question: Which of the following are benefits of extracting logic into custom hooks? (Select all that apply)
options: Cleaner component code focused on UI
blocks.explanation: Custom hooks improve reusability, testability, and component readability. However, they do not automatically optimize performance — you still need to use useMemo, useCallback, and other optimizations where appropriate.

blocks.question: What hook is used inside useFetch to ensure the fetch function reference remains stable across renders?
blocks.explanation: `useCallback` memoizes the `fetchData` function, ensuring it has the same reference across renders unless `url` changes. This prevents infinite re-fetch loops when `fetchData` is included in the useEffect dependency array.

blocks.question: Why does useLocalStorage check `typeof window === 'undefined'`?
options: To prevent errors during server-side rendering (SSR)
To check if the browser supports localStorage
To determine if the app is in development mode
blocks.explanation: During SSR (server-side rendering), `window` doesn't exist. Accessing `window.localStorage` would throw a ReferenceError. The check ensures the hook returns the initial value on the server and reads from localStorage only in the browser.

blocks.question: In the useDebounce hook, what happens to the previous timer when `value` changes before `delay` expires?
options: It continues running alongside the new timer
It is cleared by the cleanup function
blocks.explanation: The cleanup function returned by useEffect runs before the next effect execution. It calls `clearTimeout(timer)`, cancelling the previous timer. This ensures only the most recent value's timer completes, achieving the debounce behavior.

blocks.value: When to Use useReducer

`useReducer` is the go-to hook for **complex state logic** — when state transitions depend on previous state, involve multiple sub-values, or when the next state is determined by an action rather than direct assignment. It's a lightweight alternative to Redux for component-level or feature-level state.

blocks.output: The reducer handles all form state transitions through a single function. Each action is typed with a discriminated union, ensuring TypeScript checks that `SET_FIELD` includes `field` and `value`, while `SUBMIT_FAILURE` includes `errors`.

blocks.caption: useReducer centralizes state transitions: actions flow into the reducer, which returns a new state based on the action type.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A flowchart diagram showing a central box labeled 'reducer(state, action)' with arrows entering from the left labeled with actions: 'SET_FIELD', 'SUBMIT_START', 'SUBMIT_SUCCESS'. Each action arrow is a different color. The reducer box outputs 'newState' arrows to the right showing different state shapes. A feedback loop shows the new state becoming the input state for the next action. Redux-style diagram with clean lines and flat design. Purple and teal accent colors.
Using useReducer in a Component
The `useReducer` hook returns the current state and a `dispatch` function. You dispatch actions instead of calling setters directly, making state transitions predictable and testable.

blocks.output: Renders a form with username, email, and password fields. Validation errors appear inline. The submit button is disabled during submission or when the form is invalid. The reducer centralizes all state changes, making the component logic clean and the state transitions predictable.

blocks.value: useReducer vs useState

Choose `useReducer` when: state logic is complex, the next state depends on the previous one, or you're managing multiple related state values. Choose `useState` for simple, independent values. Many apps use both — `useState` for simple local state and `useReducer` for complex feature state.

blocks.output: useState is ideal for simple toggles and form inputs. useReducer excels when multiple state values must change together atomically — like a shopping cart where adding an item updates the items array, recalculates the total, and checks for free shipping eligibility.

blocks.question: What does useReducer return?
options: The current state and a dispatch function
The current state and a setState function
An array of all previous states
blocks.explanation: useReducer returns a tuple: `[state, dispatch]`. The `state` is the current state value, and `dispatch` is a function that sends actions to the reducer to trigger state transitions.

blocks.question: Which of the following are advantages of useReducer over useState? (Select all that apply)
options: Better for complex state with multiple sub-values
Easier to test state logic in isolation
blocks.explanation: useReducer centralizes state logic in a pure reducer function, making it ideal for complex state and easy to test independently (just call the reducer with a state and action). It does not automatically persist state — that requires a custom hook.

blocks.question: What TypeScript pattern is used to ensure each action object has the correct properties based on its type?
blocks.explanation: A discriminated union uses a common literal property (like `type`) to distinguish between action shapes. TypeScript narrows the union based on the `type` value, ensuring `SET_FIELD` has `field` and `value`, while `SUBMIT_FAILURE` has `errors`.

blocks.question: In the form reducer, what does `const { [action.field]: _, ...restErrors } = state.errors` do?
options: It adds a new error to the errors object
It removes the specified field from the errors object
blocks.explanation: This is a destructuring pattern that removes a dynamic key from an object. The key matching `action.field` is captured into `_` (convention for unused variable) and excluded from `restErrors`, effectively deleting that error from the state.

blocks.question: When should you prefer useReducer over useState?
options: Always — useReducer is the modern standard
When state logic is complex or involves multiple related values
blocks.explanation: useReducer is preferred when state logic is complex, the next state depends on the previous one, or multiple state values must update together. For simple independent values like toggles or single inputs, useState is simpler and more appropriate.

parts.partTitle: Part 15: Rules of Hooks and Performance

blocks.value: The Rules of Hooks

React hooks have two inviolable rules enforced by the `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` linter. Breaking these rules causes unpredictable behavior, stale closures, and infinite loops. Understanding *why* these rules exist is as important as following them.

blocks.output: The invalid component breaks Rule 1 (only call hooks at the top level). React relies on the order of hook calls to match between renders — conditionals change the call order, causing state to be assigned to wrong hooks. The fix moves the condition inside the hook.

blocks.alt: Rules of hooks diagram showing correct and incorrect hook call order
blocks.caption: React matches hooks by call order across renders. Conditionals disrupt this matching, causing state corruption.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A split-screen diagram. Left side labeled '✅ Correct': shows a vertical stack of numbered boxes (1: useState, 2: useEffect, 3: useState) that align perfectly between two render cycles. Right side labeled '❌ Wrong': shows the same stack but with a conditional branch that skips hook #2 on the second render, causing hooks #3 and #4 to shift up and receive wrong state. Red X marks on mismatched hooks. Warning signs and arrows. Educational infographic style.
useMemo and useCallback

`useMemo` memoizes expensive computations. `useCallback` memoizes function references. Both prevent unnecessary work on re-renders, but they come with a cost — only use them when profiling shows a real performance issue. Premature optimization adds complexity without benefit.

blocks.output: `filteredAndSorted` only recalculates when `products`, `filter`, or `sortBy` change — not on every render. `handleDelete` maintains the same reference across renders, preventing `ProductItem` from re-rendering unnecessarily if it's wrapped in React.memo.

blocks.value: React.memo for Component Memoization

`React.memo` wraps a component to prevent re-rendering if props haven't changed. It performs a shallow comparison by default. For complex props, provide a custom comparison function. Use it on components that receive stable props but re-render due to parent updates.

blocks.output: Clicking the increment button re-renders Parent, but ProductItem does NOT re-render because its props (product and onDelete) haven't changed. The custom comparison function ensures only relevant property changes trigger updates.

blocks.question: What is the first Rule of Hooks?
options: Only call hooks at the top level of your function
Only call hooks inside class components
Only call hooks once per component
blocks.explanation: Rule 1: Only call hooks at the top level. Don't call hooks inside loops, conditions, or nested functions. This ensures hooks are called in the same order on every render, which is how React matches state to hooks.

blocks.question: Which of the following scenarios justify using useMemo? (Select all that apply)
options: Expensive calculations that depend on specific props/state
Creating objects/arrays that are used in dependency arrays
blocks.explanation: useMemo is justified for expensive computations, creating stable object references for dependency arrays, and processing large datasets. Simple operations like string concatenation are faster than useMemo's overhead.

blocks.question: What hook memoizes a function reference to prevent child components from re-rendering?
blocks.explanation: `useCallback` returns a memoized version of the callback that only changes if one of the dependencies has changed. This is essential when passing callbacks to optimized child components that rely on reference equality.

blocks.question: What does React.memo do by default?
options: It does a deep comparison of all props
It does a shallow comparison of props
It prevents all re-renders regardless of prop changes
blocks.explanation: React.memo performs a shallow comparison of props by default. If you need deep comparison or custom logic, you provide a comparison function as the second argument.

blocks.question: Why is it wrong to call a hook inside a conditional statement?
options: It causes a syntax error in TypeScript
It breaks React's ability to match hooks to state across renders
It makes the component render faster
It prevents the component from unmounting
blocks.explanation: React matches hooks to state by their call order. If a hook is inside a conditional, the call order changes between renders when the condition changes. This causes React to associate the wrong state with the wrong hook, leading to bugs.
